_what: Every PolicyEngine analysis whose comparables search is recorded in this repository, keyed by its sources/ directory. Generated by `python -m scorecard_db.comparables index` from the directories themselves; policyengine-app-v2 and PolicyEngine/newsletters read it to check an entry's comparables. A listing means the record passed the gate.

comparisons.title: Removing the childcare cliff-edge: impacts and cost of reform
comparisons.sign_convention: positive = yield to the Exchequer (Table 4.2 notes: 'negative = cost to the Exchequer')
comparisons.estimate_label: Static cost of the 30 funded hours, both limits removed, 2027-28
comparisons.cause: The published run's Microcosm release drew each family's use of the extended hours with a mean of about 15 of the 30 weekly hours (microcosm#1126, which derives DfE's mean as about 28.5), so the static cost of the 30 hours is about half what CenTax's take-up implies. The dashboard's own full-use sensitivity adds £0.60bn in 2027-28 and £0.70bn in 2029-30 (results.json budget.sensitivities.effects_bn.full_30_hour_usage). Reruns on later, uncertified releases with the corrected draw (uk-childcare-100k-threshold#8, 22 October 2026) put the 30-hours cost at £0.96bn in 2027-28 and £1.12bn in 2029-30 as shipped, and £0.87bn and £0.96bn on CenTax's basis (no hours for reception children, DfE's funding rates, pension contributions deducted from income, 9-11-month-olds added).

comparisons.title: Removing the childcare cliff-edge: impacts and cost of reform
comparisons.sign_convention: positive = yield to the Exchequer (Table 4.2 notes: 'negative = cost to the Exchequer')
comparisons.cause: CenTax's net fiscal cost is for the free hours alone and adds two responses: parents who stop holding income below £100,000 (bunching) and partners who enter work (Table 4.2 and notes). The dashboard's net figure covers both schemes and models the labour-supply response only; it lists bunching as not modelled (results.json labour_supply.not_modelled). The two measure different things; the like-for-like comparison is CenTax's static cost.
comparisons.pe_missing: CenTax's net fiscal cost covers the free hours alone and adds bunching (parents no longer holding income below £100,000) and partners entering work; the dashboard's net figure covers both schemes and models only the labour-supply response, not bunching.

comparisons.title: Technical Appendix: underlying modelling and analysis for each of the policies in the Rates and Wrongs paper
comparisons.sign_convention: positive = yield to the Exchequer (the tables report the projected net fiscal impact)
comparisons.estimate_label: Cost of both schemes net of the labour-supply response (central elasticities), 2026-27
comparisons.cause: Both figures are the net fiscal effect of removing both limits after behavioural responses, and they have opposite signs: CBP finds a net gain to the Exchequer, the dashboard a net cost. CBP's gain comes from parents who stop holding income below £100,000, through pension contributions (Table 2) or hours worked (Table 3). The dashboard does not model that bunching response (results.json labour_supply.not_modelled) and starts from a static cost that the hours draw understates (microcosm#1126).
